articles.title: Why America’s AI data center companies are turning to airplane ‘graveyards’
articles.summary: At a time when the artificial intelligence (AI) boom has sparked a surge in electricity demand, American AI data centre companies are finding new ways to
articles.body: At a time when the artificial intelligence (AI) boom has sparked a surge in electricity demand, American AI data centre companies are finding new ways to power their infrastructure. While some are turning towards massive solar and wind farms, others are striking deals to use nuclear power to keep the servers running. Now, they are reportedly turning to Arizona’s Sonoran desert where thousands of retired airplanes with jet engines mounted sit in vast metal graveyards. Those turbines are being resurrected to keep the servers running. The New York Times reported that a growing roster of engineering firms is stripping engines from decommissioned aircraft and converting them into stationary electrical generators with data center operators snapping them up as fast as they can be built.“They’re getting creative. Just a few years ago, a traditional data center would have been like, ‘Are you kidding me? This is ridiculous’,” said Bill Kleyman, chief executive of AI platform and infrastructure provider Apolo. Today, attitudes have fundamentally shifted around project lead times. Data center developers are now singularly obsessed with "speed to power," Kleyman explained, adding, “It’s like, ‘How fast can you get me energy?’”The rush to secure self-contained energy sources has also been accelerated by political pressure. With rapid data centre construction driving public backlash over rising household utility bills, President Donald Trump has pushed facilities to generate their own power rather than pulling from local grids.“It was my idea. Data centers now are mandated by me that they build their own electricity, so they’re not taking it from the grid,” Trump told reporters in August.Tapping massive ‘power reserves’Aircraft graveyards offer an enormous, untapped energy reserve, the report pointed out. In January, the federal Energy Information Administration estimated that the engines housed inside 4,000 retired military jets parked at a single desert base in Tucson could produce 40,000 megawatts of electricity, exceeding the generation capacity of the entire state of Arizona.Converted aircraft turbines, however, come with major engineering trade-offs. For example, repurposed jet engines are generally less fuel-efficient than turbines built specifically for modern gas-fired power plants. Moreover, because of their lower operational efficiency, data centers require a higher number of jet-powered units to produce the equivalent electrical output. Converted engines release significantly higher volumes of air pollutants into surrounding communities.Elon Musk’s AI venture, xAI, has already integrated eight converted jet turbines to power a major data center in Mississippi, according to state regulatory filings and satellite imagery reviewed by The New York Times. State permits granted to the facility allow the converted turbines to emit carbon monoxide at double the rate permitted for other on-site turbines, along with a 25% higher ceiling for volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Both substances present serious health hazards.Environmental organisations and community advocates argue that leaning on older, dirtier turbines undermines clean energy goals. The Southern Environmental Law Center has formally challenged Mississippi’s regulatory approval of xAI’s turbines, arguing that the equipment maker has failed to supply documentation proving compliance with standards for toxins like formaldehyde, while accusing xAI of undercounting its projected emissions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Indian-American Aruna Miller wins re-election as Maryland lieutenant governor
articles.summary: Indian-American Aruna Miller has won re-election as Maryland's lieutenant governor after NBC News projected Democratic Governor Wes Moore's victory in the
articles.body: Indian-American Aruna Miller has won re-election as Maryland's lieutenant governor after NBC News projected Democratic Governor Wes Moore's victory in the 2026 US midterm elections. Miller, who contested alongside Moore, defeated Republican candidate Rob Krop, running mate of former state delegate Dan Cox.Miller's victory ensures another term in the state's executive office and continued Indian-American representation in US state leadership.Ahead of the election, Miller had urged Americans, particularly immigrant communities, to vote and hold the Trump-Vance administration accountable. Speaking to ANI on Election Day, she said voters were anxious about federal policies, rising fuel prices, job losses and immigration restrictions."People are feeling really anxious about the many things that are happening at the national level, but here's what I'm hopeful for. I am out here at the polls and early voting, we've had the biggest turnout of any gubernatorial election in the state of Maryland. And here at the polls, there's lots of lines here, so that tells me people are very hopeful," Miller said.She said Maryland had lost 31,000 federal jobs, affecting families and the local economy. She also criticised Trump's tariff policy, saying American consumers would ultimately bear the additional costs."A tariff is not a tax or something that another country pays. It's a tax that the consumers here pay, because ultimately, all those tariffs are going to be passed down to the consumer. So that means all the products we buy are much more expensive," she said.Miller also flagged rising fuel prices, linking them to the ongoing conflict."We're in a war of choice, that is going to raise the price every time you go to the gas station. Gas was less than USD 3 a gallon before, now it's close to USD 5 a gallon. So all this adds up to the prices and the affordability and why people are feeling anxious," she said.Miller raises concerns over immigration policiesThe lieutenant governor said federal immigration policies were creating fear among immigrant communities, international students and skilled foreign workers, including H-1B visa holders."I think they're also concerned because you see what the immigration policies that the federal administration is doing right now, when it comes to H-1B visas or even our international students, all of them are being impacted by this. And furthermore, just the attacks on immigrant communities alone with ICE agents. So there's a lot of fear here," she said.She urged voters to elect representatives who could act as a check on the administration."This is our opportunity to come out and vote, vote for a Congress and vote for a Senate that'll be the firewall against Donald Trump, and it's also our opportunity to hold the Trump-Vance administration accountable for the things that are happening," Miller said.Miller also highlighted Maryland's efforts to protect immigrant communities, including its ban on agreements under Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. The provision allows local law enforcement agencies to assist federal authorities with certain immigration enforcement functions.She said the state had also established an office of immigrant affairs to help immigrants access government services and resources.On the administration's record, Miller cited efforts to address child poverty, opioid overdoses and crime. She also highlighted diversity in the state cabinet, saying 50 per cent of cabinet secretaries were women and 50 per cent were people of colour.The 2026 US midterm elections are being held halfway through President Donald Trump's four-year term. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are being contested nationally.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Massachusetts woman found $28,260 missing from her bank account after a gas company allegedly withdrew money for a bill she did not owe
articles.summary: A Massachusetts woman was left facing an unexpected financial crisis after National Grid allegedly withdrew $28,260.60 from her bank account to cover a
articles.body: A Massachusetts woman was left facing an unexpected financial crisis after National Grid allegedly withdrew $28,260.60 from her bank account to cover a gas bill that the company had previously acknowledged was incorrect. Madison Wise, from Malden, found herself with a negative bank balance after the money was taken, leaving her unable to pay for everyday essentials. The incident came weeks after she had contacted the utility company about the unusually large bill and was reportedly assured that she owed nothing.A Massachusetts woman ended up with a $28,260 gas billAccording to CBS News Boston, Wise's troubles began in April 2026 when she opened a National Grid account in her name for a new apartment her family was preparing to move into. However, the family never got the opportunity to settle into the property. Before they could move in, the building was condemned and the lease was terminated.The utility account had been registered in Wise's name for just 3 days, making the size of the subsequent bill particularly alarming. Despite the brief period, she received a gas bill amounting to $28,260.60.The amount was far beyond what she could reasonably have expected for such a short period. Wise contacted National Grid because she believed there had been a mistake. During her initial conversation with the company, a representative reportedly told her that the bill was hers.Wise questioned the explanation, pointing out that the amount was comparable to the price of a new car and far more money than she had ever seen in one place. After further checking, however, the representative discovered that the bill had been generated because of an incorrect meter reading.The company representative reportedly confirmed that the bill was wrong and that Wise owed nothing. Believing the matter had been settled, she thought she could put the incident behind her.The withdrawal that left her bank account overdrawnThe situation took a more serious turn several weeks later when Wise woke up to discover that National Grid had withdrawn the entire $28,260.60 from her checking account.According to CBS News Boston, the unexpected debit pushed her account into a negative balance. The withdrawal was particularly damaging because the company had already informed her that the original charge was based on a faulty meter reading and that she had no outstanding balance.Money that was meant to cover essential household expenses had effectively disappeared from her account.Wise said she could no longer make ordinary purchases, including groceries and fuel for her car. The situation also raised concerns about other payments that were scheduled to leave her account automatically. With her rent due within a week, she feared that the unexpected negative balance would cause further financial problems.Why did the delayed refund create such a serious problemThe withdrawal affected more than Wise's bank balance. She was caring for her 2-year-old child and was also pregnant at the time, making access to money particularly important for her family's everyday needs.Speaking to CBS News Boston, she described the experience as an overwhelming period of panic. She was worried about being unable to buy food, fill her car with petrol or pay for necessary medical appointments during her pregnancy.When she contacted National Grid again, she was reportedly informed that returning the money could take between seven and 10 days. For someone whose account had been pushed into the negative by a withdrawal of more than $28,000, the proposed waiting period was a major concern. Wise explained that the company did not initially appear to understand the scale of the problem.National Grid responds after the woman contacts local reportersAfter struggling to get the issue resolved, Wise approached CBS Boston's I-Team Call for Action, a consumer assistance initiative that investigates complaints and helps people deal with companies.The intervention appeared to bring a rapid change in the company's response. Wise told CBS that within approximately two hours of contacting the programme, she received a call from National Grid's president's office.During the call, the company apologised for the trouble caused and assured her that it would take steps to return the money. Wise said she was told that the refund would be sent immediately.National Grid subsequently issued a statement acknowledging the impact of the incident and apologising to its customer. The company said it had refunded the charge and was working with Wise's bank to ensure the money was returned as quickly as possible.It also said it was reviewing the account to understand what had caused the error and was working directly with Wise to make sure the matter was fully resolved.The company indicated that the process of getting the funds back into her account could take two to three days, a shorter timeframe than the seven to 10 days initially communicated to her.The company agrees to cover additional financial consequencesThe response also included measures intended to address the financial difficulties caused by the withdrawal. According to CBS News Boston, Wise told the I-Team that National Grid had agreed to cover any overdraft fees and bounced cheques resulting from the incident.The utility also offered to provide credits to her account. She said the incident had made her question whether the same thing could happen to other customers.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US midterms: Democrats flip 4 Governor, 22 House & 6 Senate seats as blue wave surges
articles.summary: Democrats made significant gains in the 2026 US midterm elections, flipping Republican-held seats in the House of Representatives, capturing a key Senate
articles.body: Democrats made significant gains in the 2026 US midterm elections, flipping Republican-held seats in the House of Representatives, capturing a key Senate seat in North Carolina and winning the Georgia governorship.The results mark a setback for President Donald Trump's Republican Party, which entered the elections controlling both chambers of Congress and the White House. The gains could reshape the balance of power in Washington for the final two years of Trump's term.House: Democrats flip key Republican-held seatsDemocrats have flipped 25 Republican-held seats in the US House of Representatives, making gains across four states. The victories include:California1st Congressional District: Democrat Mike McGuire defeated Republican incumbent James Gallagher. The result follows mid-decade redistricting under Proposition 50. Gallagher had won a June 2026 special election to fill the vacancy left by Doug LaMalfa's death, defeating McGuire.3rd Congressional District: Democrat Ami Bera defeated Republican Robb Tucker in a redrawn district previously represented by Republican Kevin Kiley. This is a redistricting-related pickup, not a conventional incumbent defeat.Colorado (1 flip)8th Congressional District: Democrat Manny Rutinel defeated Republican incumbent Gabe Evans, reclaiming the seat Republicans had won in 2024.Wisconsin3rd Congressional District: Democrat Rebecca Cooke defeated Republican incumbent Derrick Van Orden, flipping the seat for her party. Cooke won 52.4% of the vote (172,757) against Van Orden's 45.8% (150,872). She had narrowly lost to Van Orden in the 2024 election.Indiana (1 flip)5th Congressional District: Democrat J.D. Ford defeated Republican incumbent Victoria Spartz.Senate: 6 seats flipped in favour of DemocratsDemocrats have flipped two Republican-held Senate seats, winning in North Carolina and South Carolina.North Carolina: Democrat Roy Cooper defeated Republican Michael Whatley, flipping the seat held by retiring Republican Senator Thom Tillis.Texas: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat in decades to win a US Senate seat since 1988.Ohio: Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican incumbent Jon Husted, wresting the US Senate seat from Republican control and returning to the chamber after losing his re-election bid in 2024.South Carolina: Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, flipping the seat previously held by her brother.Kansas: Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, flipping the US Senate seat from Republican to Democratic control. Hamilton, a pastor and author, founded the Church of the Resurrection in 1990, which has grown into the largest United Methodist congregation in the US.Iowa: Democrat Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson, flipping the Senate seat held by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Turek, a former Paralympic wheelchair basketball player, has represented Iowa in the state legislature since 2023.Governor: Democrats flip 4 seatsDemocrats have flipped three Republican-held governorship so farGeorgia: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, ending more than two decades of Republican control of the governor's office. She will succeed term-limited Republican Governor Brian Kemp and become the first Black woman elected governor of a US state.Iowa: Democrat Rob Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn, ending Republican control of the governor's office. He will succeed Republican Governor Kim Reynolds, who did not seek re-election, and become the state's first Democratic governor since 2011.Ohio: Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, flipping the governor's office from Republican to Democratic control. She will succeed term-limited Republican Governor Mike DeWine and become Ohio's first Democratic governor since 2007.Texas: Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, ending 32 years of Republican control of the governor's office. She will become the state's first Latina governor.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Tennessee woman claimed she was a wounded Marine who survived an Afghanistan ambush; she used the story to obtain GoFundMe donations and was jailed
articles.summary: A Tennessee woman who claimed to be a wounded US Marine Corps veteran has pleaded guilty to fraud.
articles.body: A Tennessee woman who claimed to be a wounded US Marine Corps veteran has pleaded guilty to fraud. The US Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Tennessee, Amanda Kate Walker Bass, 36, of Fayette County, said she was the lone survivor of a 2010 ambush in Afghanistan. The office says she never served in the armed forces. A GoFundMe page was set up for her benefit, and she shared the story online to gain donations, free labour and other benefits. She pleaded guilty to wire fraud and fraudulent use of military medals, and is due to be sentenced on 14 May 2026.What did she claim about surviving an Afghanistan ambush in 2010According to the US Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Tennessee, Bass claimed to be a multiple-time deployed US Marine Corps veteran. The release says she also presented herself as the lone survivor of an enemy ambush in Afghanistan in 2010, and that she claimed the ambush had left her seriously wounded.The office describes this account as a fictitious narrative. It says Bass used the story for financial gain. The release does not attribute any other motive to her and does not name any other military unit, location or event connected to the claims.What did The Daily Memphian report about Bass in its 2021 articleThe press release states that a GoFundMe page was set up for Bass's benefit. It adds that she shared the story online and elsewhere in order to gain donations, free labour and other benefits. The release does not give the amount raised or say who set up the page.The office also says that in July 2021 Bass induced The Daily Memphian to publish an article about her. According to the release, the article was headlined "Disabled, legally blind veteran now dealer of luxury goods". The release repeats that Bass never served in the armed forces.What did prosecutors say about her fake military claimsUS District Judge Mark S. Norris is due to sentence Bass on 14 May 2026, according to the release. For the wire fraud conviction, she faces up to 20 years in prison and a fine of $250,000. For the conviction for fraudulent use of military medals, she faces up to one year in prison and a fine of $100,000.Dunavant said that fraudulently claiming military service or medals for unjust personal enrichment victimises military heroes and preys on the trust citizens place in veterans of the US Armed Forces. In his words, "It is offensive, and it is illegal." He added that his office looked forward to imposing a real consequence on the defendant. The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation. Assistant United States Attorney William C. Bateman III prosecuted it on behalf of the United States.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After admitting 'hardest year' yet in its 13-year history, Canva announces major job cuts; CEO sends long 'layoff email'
articles.summary: Canva, the Australian design software company has announced a major job cuts at the company.
articles.body: Canva, the Australian design software company has announced a major job cuts at the company. This restructuring effort of the company will affect 1,271 employees, or about 22% of its global workforce, with co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins describing the move as "the hardest moment" in the company's 13-year history. The graphic design platform revealed the changes in a lengthy message to employees that was later published on the company's newsroom website. The announcement comes as Canva grapples with slowing growth and seeks to reshape its organisation for what it calls its next chapter. Perkins apologised to those affected for the pain and disruption.CEO calls it Canva's toughest yearIn the note, Perkins said the company had reached a difficult conclusion after months of reviewing its future direction. She acknowledged that the restructuring would result in layoffs, role changes, and relocation requests for some employees. "This has been our hardest year yet," Perkins wrote, adding that Canva's growth had slowed for the first time in a decade. According to the CEO, the company explored several alternatives before determining that smaller adjustments would not be enough to prepare the business for long-term success. She said the company needed to "refound Canva" by returning to its roots of smaller, empowered teams with greater ownership and autonomy.Canva layoffs: 22% of workforce affectedCanva said 1,271 people, representing roughly 22% of its workforce, will be affected by the changes. While some employees will leave the company, others may be asked to relocate to centralised hubs or transition into new roles. Perkins noted that the restructuring would impact people across teams and geographies. The company currently operates across 37 countries, with employees spread across a global network of offices and remote locations.Support package for affected employeesThe company has outlined a support package for affected workers. Canva said departing employees will receive at least six months of salary, including statutory entitlements, regardless of location. Other benefits include up to 12 months of healthcare coverage where applicable, career coaching, interview preparation, LinkedIn Premium subscriptions and access to an alumni talent network. Employees leaving the company will also be allowed to keep their Canva-issued MacBooks. In addition, the company is launching a Canva Collective Fund that will provide grants of US$10,000 to eligible departing employees interested in starting businesses or community projects.Major organisational overhaul plannedAs part of the restructuring, Canva will merge its Product, Growth and Platform divisions into a single Product Organisation. The company said the move is intended to reduce internal handovers, simplify decision-making and provide teams with clearer ownership over projects. Canva is also reducing specialisation across certain functions, collapsing management layers and consolidating overlapping responsibilities. The company believes broader roles will allow teams to take end-to-end responsibility for their work rather than operating within narrower areas of expertise.Another key change involves location strategy. Canva said Sydney will become the primary base for more of its product teams, and some employees will be asked to relocate. Beginning in January, most hybrid employees will also be expected to spend two to three days each week in the officeRead Canva CEO Melanie Perkins’ email to employees hereHi everyone,Today, I have some profoundly difficult news to share.After months of thinking through how to set Canva up for the next chapter, we have made the incredibly hard decision to make significant changes to how we’re organised, where some of our teams are based, and the roles and skills we need for the future.This means 1,271 people, or 22% of Canva, will be impacted. For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.This is without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history. Behind every decision is someone we care deeply about, and I know the consequences will be very real for those directly affected, their families, friends and teammates.I’m deeply sorry for the pain and disruption this will cause for everyone affected. While nothing can make this news easier, we will do everything we possibly can to support everyone affected. I want to explain as openly as I can why we're making these changes, how we reached these decisions, and, most importantly, how we will care for the people affected today.Why we’re making these changesWe've spoken a lot about how quickly the world is changing. New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use.Over the past thirteen years, we’ve turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade.After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I've come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community.It also means making some of the hardest decisions we've ever faced, including saying goodbye to people who have helped make Canva what it is today. For that, I am deeply sorry.What we’re changingWe're making three changes to bring more of what has made Canva special back into how we work.#1. We're simplifying how we come together to build CanvaAs we've grown, more of our work has become organised around team structures and narrow areas of ownership. Improving one part of our product often requires navigating between Product, Growth and Platform, with more handovers and coordination than necessary. This has made it harder to take ownership of bigger problems and to build a deeply unified product for our community. We’ve tried many ways to solve this over the years, but it’s become clear we need to revisit our underlying structure.To do that, we’re bringing Product, Growth and Platform together into one Product Org and changing the way we work to provide clearer ownership, greater autonomy and flexibility to tackle our most important goals. We want to get back to spending more time building, and less time navigating how work gets done.#2. We’re reducing subspecialisation and collapsing layers to broaden ownershipOver time, we've divided work across more and more subspecialties and teams. While this has helped us build valuable expertise, it's also fragmented ownership and made it harder to see the full picture, with different teams responsible for many pieces of the same work.We're reducing this fragmentation and incorporating narrower subspecialties into broader roles so teams have more ownership of goals from start to finish. We're also simplifying layers, consolidating overlapping responsibilities, and ensuring teams have the right mix of skills and experience for the chapter ahead.#3. We’re co-locating closely connected teams and increasing in-person collaborationWorking across countries has brought enormous benefits and talent, but it’s also made it harder to bring the right people together to solve complex problems. We’ll continue investing in our global team, particularly where being close to our community, customers and markets matters most.At the same time, Sydney will become the primary home for more of our product teams, as well as roles in other Specialties where shared context and close collaboration are especially important. We know relocating is a big decision for those being asked to consider it, and we're committed to making the process as smooth as possible with comprehensive support.We also want to bring more teams together in person to build trust, learn from one another and strengthen the connections that make Canva special. From January, we expect most Hybrid Canvanauts to spend around 2 to 3 days in the office each week, depending on what makes sense in your area.How we approached these decisionsI know many of you will have questions about how we made these decisions. We began with one question: what does Canva need to do to succeed in the chapter ahead?We started with our mission and future goals, then considered the structures, skills and locations needed to achieve them. Only then did we look at what this would mean for individual roles. While understanding how we reached these decisions won't make them any less painful, I want to emphasise that they are not a reflection of the talent, care and dedication people have brought to Canva, their skills or the enormous contributions they've made along the way.Supporting those who are leavingWe know everyone's circumstances are different, and while nothing can make today’s news easy, we've tried to reflect those different needs in the financial, career and wellbeing support we're providing to everyone affected:•Everyone will receive at least six months of salary, inclusive of statutory entitlements, regardless of location. •Removing the one-year vesting cliff for those who joined in the past year. •Twelve months of continued healthcare coverage in countries where we currently provide this. •Twelve months of Canva Care (our EAP), with this coverage also extending to family members. •Dedicated career support, including one-on-one coaching, interview preparation, and one year of LinkedIn Premium. We're also dedicating a significant portion of our Talent Acquisition team to helping people review their resumes and practice for interviews to find their next opportunity. •An opt-in alumni talent directory that we'll proactively share with our investors, partners, and wider industry network to help connect departing Canvanauts with new roles. •Everyone leaving will be able to keep their Canva MacBook as we know not everyone has a personal laptop. We’re also launching the Canva Collective Fund, providing US$10,000 grants to departing Canvanauts who want to start something of their own. Whether it’s starting a business or doing something meaningful for their local community, the fund is designed to help get those ideas off the ground. Everyone leaving as part of these changes will have until the 14 of December to register their interest, and we won’t take any ownership or equity in what they create.What happens nextOur immediate priority is to make time for the conversations with everyone directly impacted by these changes. Those impacted will receive a calendar invite for an individual meeting with a senior leader in their area to discuss the next steps and support available should they wish to attend.With teams across 37 countries, we'll need to follow different local requirements and processes, which means the timing and way these conversations happen may vary depending on where people are based.We also want to give everyone the time to process this news and say goodbye in their own way. Everyone leaving Canva will continue to have access to Slack and Gmail until the end of the week, so they can choose when and how to share the news with their teams. This means you may not know exactly how your team is changing straight away, and we ask everyone to respect the privacy of those having these conversations. Leads will share more about the changes to different areas by the end of the week.We've put together some answers to common questions and everything you need to know. There's no need to read through everything right now, but we hope they'll be helpful whenever you're ready. Next week, we’ll come together for a Company All Hands on November 10th to talk through these changes, answer questions, and share more about the path ahead. We’ve asked Org Leads to wait until after this to bring their teams together, with Org All Hands taking place from November 11th.To everyone continuing at Canva: I know this news will be incredibly difficult, especially as we say goodbye to friends and teammates who have been such an important part of our journey. Please look after yourselves and one another and be there for those who are leaving. We’re also cancelling non-critical meetings for the rest of the week, and encourage anyone who needs some time and space to process this news to take the day off. There’s no need to log this as leave.To those who will be leaving Canva: I wish I could adequately express how grateful I am for everything you've contributed. The Canva that exists today is the result of your hard work, creativity, passion and care. Hundreds of millions of people around the world have been empowered by what you've helped build, and I hope you know just how much of a difference you've made. I am deeply sorry this is how your chapter at Canva is ending. Please know these decisions do not diminish your talent, the value of your contributions, or the difference you've made here. We will do everything we can to support you in what comes next, and I hope the work we do from here will be worthy of what you've helped build.MelYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Telugu-origin Aruna Miller re-elected as Maryland LG; Saritha Komatireddy loses NY AG race
articles.summary: HYDERABAD: Telugu-origin Aruna Miller has been re-elected as Maryland’s lieutenant governor for a second four-year term, alongside Democratic Governor Wes
articles.body: HYDERABAD: Telugu-origin Aruna Miller has been re-elected as Maryland’s lieutenant governor for a second four-year term, alongside Democratic Governor Wes Moore, after the Associated Press projected a victory for the Democratic ticket. In New York, incumbent Democrat Letitia James won a third term as attorney general, defeating Republican challenger Saritha Komatireddy, according to Times Union.Miller contested alongside Moore, who defeated Republican challenger Dan Cox, with Rob Krop as his running mate. The Associated Press and Wes Moore and Miller’s campaign page called the Maryland governor-lieutenant governor race for the Moore-Miller ticket. In a post-election statement issued by the campaign, Miller said, “Governor Moore and I are incredibly grateful to Marylanders for trusting us once again. To our tireless volunteers, dedicated campaign teams, and families who sacrificed so much, thank you. I’ve always said I have the best job in the world because I get to serve the people of Maryland. And I can’t wait to get back to work!”In a separate statement shared with TOI, Miller said the administration had helped create nearly 100,000 jobs and welcomed more than 55,000 new businesses over the past four years. She also cited a 44% fall in homicides statewide and a 50% decline in overdose deaths from their pandemic peak.Reflecting on her journey, Miller said she had immigrated to the US at the age of seven and never imagined she would one day help lead the state she called home. “The support from the Indian American community has been especially meaningful. I hope my reelection inspires more young people, particularly those from immigrant families, to see themselves in positions of leadership and recognise that their backgrounds are a source of strength, not a limitation,” she said.In New York, James defeated Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor who contested on the Republican ticket. Election-night figures reported by Times Union put James at 65.1% and Komatireddy at 32.8%, with more than half of precincts reporting at the time. The figures were unofficial and not final certified results.Telugu-American community representatives said Miller’s re-election was a matter of pride for the community and that the participation of Telugu-origin women in public life in the US could inspire younger generations.“I personally see Aruna Miller’s public service as encouraging examples of Telugu-American participation in American civic life. Seeing women from our community pursue public leadership can inspire younger generations to see themselves as future public servants,” said Vamshi Reddy, former president of the Telangana American Telugu Association.Niranjan Srungavarapu of the Telugu Association of North America (TANA) said Miller’s re-election was a source of pride for the community. “Aruna Miller’s accomplishments as Maryland’s Lieutenant Governor are a source of pride for the broader Indian-American and Telugu-American communities. These developments reflect the growing contributions of Indian-origin Americans to public service and leadership in the United States. They also inspire younger generations to become more actively involved in civic affairs and public life,” he told TOI.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ardbeg buried two whisky casks under Islay peat for 34 months; just 456 bottles were released, and one later sold at auction for £1,350
articles.summary: Discover the unique story of Ardbeg's buried whisky casks and their limited NFT release, capturing the interest of whisky enthusiasts and collectors alike.
articles.body: Most of us have probably lost something in the dirt at some point. It might have been a ring at the beach, a charger in the garden or something else altogether. Ardbeg did something similar, but on purpose. According to The Spirits Business, the Islay distillery buried two casks of whisky in a peat bog close to its site and left them there for nearly three years. The whisky then became the distillery's first NFT, a digital token linked to a physical bottle. The team treated the process as a flavour experiment. Only 456 bottles came out of it, which made the release rare from the very beginning.Why bury whisky in a bogThe idea was the brainchild of Dr Bill Lumsden, who led whisky creation at Ardbeg at the time. In 2014, a team led by then distillery manager Mickey Heads buried two casks of mature whisky near the distillery. They were both second-fill bourbon casks, which are basically oak casks that had previously held bourbon and had already been used once to mature Scotch. The ground in question was a peat bog, and that matters. The University of St Andrews peatlands exhibition explains that peat is formed when waterlogged soil inhibits the decomposition of plant material. Ardbeg reported that this was the first time the distillery buried barrels in oxygen-depleted, waterlogged ground. The casks were kept underground for two years and 10 months, totalling 34 months. They were then dug up about three years after burial and moved back into the warehouse, where the whisky continued to mature for several more years. After that it was blended and bottled at 45.5% ABV ahead of its April 2022 release.What did the bog really change?It is hard to say exactly what the bog changed. The same trade report said the time spent underground was said to give the whisky earthy, mossy, and herbal flavours rather than the smoking intensity that is Ardbeg’s trademark. But tasting notes aren't lab results. A 1995 review in the journal Forestry by J.R. Mosedale discussed the effect of oak properties on flavour. The review also explains that their scientific understanding of how cask properties shape maturation is incomplete, but that choosing casks for the effect on flavour was still possible. This makes a buried cask hard to judge. The whisky also had extra years maturing in a warehouse after the dig, so the bog cannot take all the credit for the work.A rare bottle with a digital twist The name of the bottle was Fon Fhòid, which translates to “under the turf” in Scottish Gaelic. The release was just as unusual as the ageing process itself. It was launched on the BlockBar platform on April 19, 2022. Each of the 456 tokens represented a 70 cL bottle. Moreover, buyers could trade their tokens in the platform's marketplace. Owners of the token could start taking delivery of their bottles from BlockBar’s secure storage starting December 1, 2022. The price was 1 ETH, the cryptocurrency Ether, which was about £2,363 at the time of the release announcement.What one bottle fetched laterOne of those bottles was later part of an online whisky auction that closed on January 23, 2023. The listing noted that the owners needed to redeem the NFT to receive the physical bottle, one of the 456 numbered bottles. The final bid was £1,350. That’s about 43% less than the launch price of about £2,363, but the numbers weren’t a perfect match. Ether’s value often changes, and there can be additional fees on top of auction sales. So, one sale suggests very little on its own. It does suggest, however, that a rare bottle might not always fetch a higher price later. The real attraction is the story behind it. Ardbeg turned a patch of wet ground on Islay into a flavour experiment, and 456 bottles carried that story forward.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Man paid premium a day before his Bolero was stolen, but insurer rejected claim citing policy issuance date; consumer court orders full Rs 3.5 lakh insurance payout, 9% interest and Rs 25,000 compensation
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Punjab has directed an insurance company to pay Rs 3.5 lakh to a man whose Mahindra Bolero pickup was stolen.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Punjab has directed an insurance company to pay Rs 3.5 lakh to a man whose Mahindra Bolero pickup was stolen. It held that the insurer could not reject the claim on the ground that the policy was issued after the theft, since the premium had been paid a day earlier through the financier.Case backgroundAs per the commission order, Jatinder Kumar, the complainant, owned a Mahindra Bolero pickup, financed through Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company. He insured it with Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Company for September 8, 2021, to September 7, 2022, paying a premium of Rs 21,103. The insured declared value (IDV) was Rs 3.5 lakh.The vehicle was stolen from outside his house on the intervening night of September 7 and 8, 2021. An FIR was registered at Sadar police station, Hoshiarpur, on September 8. The police could not trace the vehicle, and later the court also accepted their untraced report.Kumar then lodged a claim with the insurer. He alleged that he was informed orally that the claim had been rejected because he reported the theft 21 days late, but he received no formal letter of the same.However, the insurer’s written repudiation, dated February 17, 2022, told a different story. It alleged “deliberate and wilful misrepresentation” about the date of theft and the cause of loss, though the commission would later find no evidence of any such misrepresentation.Kumar approached the commission, alleging deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. He named the finance company only as a necessary party and sought no relief against it.In its written statement before the commission, the insurer argued that the vehicle was not insured at the time of theft. It said the theft occurred around 2 am on September 8, 2021, while the policy period began at 1.58pm that day.Commission’s findingsThe bench of president Naveen Puri and member Harvimal Dogra found that the insurer had led no evidence of any misrepresentation, and that the FIR was registered on the day of the theft. It set aside the repudiation letter.It also held that the “policy issued after theft” argument was not in the repudiation letter. Citing the Supreme Court’s rulings in Saurashtra Chemicals v. National Insurance Co. and JSK Industries v. Oriental Insurance Co., it said an insurer cannot go beyond the grounds stated in its repudiation.Anil Kumar Patial, branch manager of the finance company, testified that the comp;lainant completed formalities on September 6, 2021, and the vehicle was physically inspected on September 7. He added that the premium was collected in cash that day and the policy was punched with the insurer. The finance company’s file, produced as evidence, carried photographs and time-stamped inspection records."Thus, after perusing the evidence of Anil Kumar Patial and the copy of the complete file Ex. CX, it becomes crystal clear that the insurance premium was paid by the complainant prior to the theft only," the bench said.The commission noted that the finance company was named as an “intermediary” on the policy and that the two companies are sister concerns. It held the next-day issuance resulted from dealings between them and that the insurer led no evidence that the premium was received after the theft.It relied on the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling in National Insurance Co. v. Maya Devi, which held that an insurer cannot escape liability once the premium is paid before the incident. It rejected the insurer’s reliance on Reliance Life Insurance v. Jaya Wadhwani, saying that case involved a life policy and a cheque premium not yet realised, whereas Kumar paid in cash.Final orderAnnounced on October 28, 2026, the order partly allowed the complaint. The commission directed the insurer to pay:Rs 3.5 lakh, the IDV, with 9 percent annual interest from February 17, 2022, until realisationRs 25,000 as compensation for hardshipRs 10,000 as litigation expensesPayment must be made within 45 days, failing which an additional 2 percent penal interest per annum from February 17, 2022, will apply over and above the 9 percent.

articles.title: A Washington man was due to inherit his father's ranch, but a court found he had financially abused his father and the land went to his children; 14 years later, an appeals court upheld $166,698.50 in divorce judgments
articles.summary: Calvin Evans Jr.
articles.body: Calvin Evans Jr. expected to inherit his father’s Washington ranch, a property that had also become central to his divorce from Deborah Evans, now Deborah Bunney. During the couple’s 2011 dissolution, a court awarded Bunney the full $174,000 the marital community had invested in improvements to the ranch, based on the expectation that Evans would receive the property from his father. But a separate probate dispute later found that Evans had financially abused his father, leaving him with nothing from the estate and sending the ranch to Evans’s four adult children. Fourteen years after the divorce judgments were entered, Evans asked a court to undo them because the anticipated inheritance never arrived. On November 2, 2026, the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One, refused. It upheld two divorce judgments totalling $166,698.50 against Evans, along with a 2021 order extending them, concluding that his challenge came too late and that the loss of the inheritance was not an extraordinary circumstance justifying relief, as per Justia U.S. Law. Read more details about it here:The ranch and the divorceEvans and Bunney lived and worked on the ranch owned by Evans’s father during the later years of their marriage. The marital community invested at least $174,000 in improvements to the property. Evans’s father’s 2006 will left the ranch to Evans, and that expected inheritance became a major factor in the couple’s divorce.The dissolution court entered its decree on September 15, 2011. Because it found Evans would retain more than $800,000 in ranch property, it awarded Bunney the entire $174,000 community investment. The decree included two monetary judgments against Evans, one for $162,190.50 and another for $4,508, bringing the principal total to $166,698.50.The decree treated the ranch as Evans’s property only if he inherited it from his father, subject to Bunney’s $174,000 lien. It also said the court retained jurisdiction to reconsider the financial distribution if Evans did not succeed under his father’s will but received property through intestate succession or another route.The inheritance falls apartWhile the divorce was still pending, Evans’s three siblings filed a petition under Washington’s Trust and Estate Disputed Resolution Act, known as TEDRA. They sought to invalidate the will on grounds including lack of testamentary capacity and undue influence, and asked the court to declare Evans an abuser under the applicable statute, which would prevent him from inheriting his father’s property.On May 31, 2012, the TEDRA court found that Evans had financially abused his father. As a result, Evans received nothing from his father’s estate, and the ranch passed to Evans’s four adult children. The Washington Court of Appeals later affirmed that decision in 2015.The property did not disappear from Evans’s financial life entirely. Two of his children, Cory and Jesse Evans, later transferred their combined 50 percent interest in the ranch to Hidden River Ranch LLC, a company Evans solely owned, in exchange for his agreement to leave each child 50 percent of any ranch interest he held. That arrangement meant that, although Evans did not inherit the land directly, his company acquired half of it through his children.Evans tries to undo the judgmentsAfter losing the TEDRA appeal, Evans moved in May 2017 to vacate the two 2011 divorce judgments and redistribute the couple’s property. The dissolution court denied the motion without prejudice, saying it needed more information about the outcome of Bunney’s separate unjust-enrichment lawsuit against the estate and those who ultimately inherited the ranch.That separate lawsuit ultimately failed. In March 2019, the court dismissed Bunney’s unjust-enrichment claims with prejudice. By then, the dissolution court had also denied Bunney’s request to place a lien on the ranch because Hidden River Ranch was not a party to the divorce case, while noting that it had previously declined to vacate the divorce judgment and maintained that position.Despite that clear signal, Evans did not renew his request to vacate the judgments. The appeals court later found that he had the information he needed by March 2019, but waited until April 2025 to file another motion for relief.The 2021 extension and the lineIn July 2021, Bunney applied to extend the 2011 judgments for another 10 years under Washington’s judgment-enforcement statute. The dissolution court granted the extension on July 16, 2021, allowing execution on the judgments during the additional period.The ranch was later ordered sold in a partition action because it could not be divided effectively. In December 2024, the partition court found that Bunney was the judgment creditor, that the principal amount of the judgments was $166,698.50, that Evans had made no payments, and that interest was accruing at 12 percent per year. The court then granted Bunney a charging lien against any portion of the sale proceeds to which Evans or his interest in Hidden River Ranch was entitled.Evans said he only learned of the 2021 extension in December 2024, when Bunney sought that lien. About five months later, in April 2025, he moved to vacate both the original judgments and the extension order.Why the appeal failedThe appeals court reviewed the trial court’s refusal to vacate the judgments for abuse of discretion. It concluded there was none. Evans’s challenge to the original 2011 judgments was untimely because he knew by 2012 that he had not inherited the ranch, and he had the information needed to renew his motion by March 2019.The court also rejected Evans’s argument that Bunney’s failure to give notice of the 2021 extension required vacating it. Under the statute, an extension is granted as a matter of right, and the limited issues a court may consider are timeliness, partial satisfaction and calculation errors. Evans did not identify a specific argument he was prevented from making, nor did he provide clear and convincing evidence that any alleged lack of notice caused him unfair prejudice.Finally, the court held that losing the anticipated inheritance was not an extraordinary circumstance under Washington’s rule for reopening judgments. The divorce decree had expressly recognised that the inheritance was uncertain and reserved jurisdiction to reconsider it. Because that risk was anticipated, its eventual occurrence did not become extraordinary merely because it happened.What the ruling meansThe decision leaves Bunney’s $166,698.50 judgment intact, with interest continuing to accrue and a charging lien connected to any proceeds from the ranch sale attributable to Evans or his company. Evans’s failure to inherit the ranch did not erase the financial obligations created in the divorce.The case is a reminder that divorce settlements built around expected inheritances can be fragile. Courts may account for an anticipated asset, but they can also preserve jurisdiction to revisit the arrangement if circumstances change. In this case, the court did exactly that, yet Evans’s long delay in seeking relief proved decisive.For families involved in probate and divorce disputes at the same time, the ruling also shows how separate cases can shape one another. A finding of financial abuse removed Evans’s inheritance, but it did not automatically undo the divorce court’s earlier decision. The Washington Court of Appeals has now affirmed that the original judgments remain enforceable.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In the 1980s, an English surgeon paid a few hundred pounds for a Chinese vase kept in the kitchen; in 2022 an expert spotted the Qianlong mark and it made £1.45M
articles.summary: Discover how a Chinese vase bought for a few hundred pounds in the 1980s was identified as valuable antique with a Qianlong mark, ultimately fetching £1.45 million at auction.
articles.body: A Chinese porcelain vase spent years as an ordinary household decoration in an English family’s home. The owner purchased it for a couple of hundred pounds decades ago, not realising that the vase was related to the imperial Court of the Qing Dynasty of China. It was kept in their kitchen without realising its potential appeal to collectors of Chinese antiques. The unique design of the vase attracted the attention of an expert in antiques, who found a six-character Qianlong seal mark on the base of the vase. This vase was sold at Dreweatts auction on 18 May 2022 for a hammer price of £1.2 million, according to the auction house. The final price reached £1,449,000 after adding the buyer's premium.An English surgeon bought the vase for a few hundred poundsDreweatts said an English surgeon bought the vase for a few hundred pounds in the 1980s. Newstead said the surgeon bought it simply because he liked how it looked. The family had no receipt, so the exact date and price of the purchase are not known. After the surgeon died, the vase passed to his son, who kept it in the kitchen of the family home in the English Midlands. The family knew nothing of its history. The porcelain was stored about 60 cm high, with a rich glaze and ornate gold and silver decoration. Cranes and bats decorated its globular body and slender neck, a shape known as tianqiuping, literally “heavenly globe”.Mark Newstead, a specialist consultant at Dreweatts, first saw the vase in the 1990s on a social visit to the family. He later recalled being surprised to find it in the kitchen and telling them it looked like something rather good. He didn't pick it up or inspect it, because that wouldn't have been appropriate for a guest.The Qianlong Mark connected the vase to 18th-century ChinaOn closer observation, the six-character seal mark was discovered on the bottom of the vase, belonging to the Qianlong emperor. This emperor was the ruler of China between 1735 and 1796 and belonged to the Qing dynasty. The mark assisted in establishing the connection between the vase and imperial porcelain from the time of this Emperor. According to Dreweatts, the item was an example of Qianlong period imperial porcelain. It was categorised as a blue-glazed, silver and gilt ‘Bat and Crane’ vase with tianqiuping form. It is also an example of the interest of the Qianlong emperor in Chinese ceramics and other historical artefacts.Decorations on the vase were also one of the reasons for its popularity. The vase was decorated with silver cranes, bearing symbols of the Eight Immortals of Daoism. Cranes and bats were depicted to express notions like longevity and good fortune, which were typical for the style preferred in the Qianlong court. Dreweatts highlighted the unusual pairing of gold decoration with slightly raised silver against the cobalt-blue glaze. It said a vase like this needed at least three kiln firings, one for each glaze and enamel: over 1200° C for the cobalt blue, then lower temperatures for the turquoise inside and the gold and silver enamels. It also knew of no other documented Tianqiuping decorated with this combination of gold and silver.Dreweatts estimated the vase at £100,000 to £150,000 After recognising its importance, Dreweatts prepared the vase for its Chinese Ceramics and Works of Art auction in Newbury, Berkshire. It puts an estimate of £100,000 to £150,000 on the vase, excluding fees. The sale took place on 18 May 2022, with bidders from China, Hong Kong, the USA and the UK taking part. Newstead said the international interest made for very competitive bidding. The vase was sold for a hammer price of £1.2 million, well above the estimated range. When the buyer's premium was considered, the vase sold for £1,449,000. An international buyer bought the vase by telephone. The official Dreweatts auction announcement records the vase’s Qianlong-period attribution, its distinctive decoration and its original auction estimate. Its Asian Art results also list the final sale price of £1,449,000.The vase’s earlier journey from China remains unknownThough the mark of the Qianlong determines the era of the vase, the previous ownership history is uncertain. There were no records of receipt or any documentation as to how the vase ended up in England from China.Dreweatts described the vase as being a piece made for the Qianlong Emperor's court. Furthermore, they believed that the size and design of the piece made it suitable for display in the Qing Dynasty Palace Hall. Still, that does not mean that the vase actually got displayed there or that the journey from China was documented. The difference between attribution and provenance of an object is significant. While the mark, along with the craftsmanship and design of the piece, helps to date a porcelain item, it does not tell the entire history of its ownership. For the surgeon’s family, the vase has been a family heirloom for many years. Its identification by an antique specialist revealed the connection to 18th-century imperial China, while an eventual auction sale turned a purchase worth a few hundred pounds into a £1,449,000 result.You use AI every day. articles.title: The family of soul legend Otis Redding opened an $11.2 million arts centre in his hometown; the facility gives young musicians recording studios and songwriting spaces
articles.summary: The family of soul music legend Otis Redding has opened an $11.2 million arts centre in his hometown of Macon, Georgia, offering young people access to
articles.body: The family of soul music legend Otis Redding has opened an $11.2 million arts centre in his hometown of Macon, Georgia, offering young people access to recording studios, songwriting rooms and musical instruments. The facility, established by the Otis Redding Foundation, provides a permanent home for the family's longstanding efforts to introduce children to music and creative expression. Opened in March 2025, the centre brings together education, performance and technology under one roof, continuing the singer's legacy while giving a new generation opportunities to explore its musical ambitions.The Otis Redding arts centre is helping young musiciansAccording to the Macon Telegraph's report, the Otis Redding Center for the Arts covers approximately 15,000 square feet in downtown Macon. Its modern design incorporates 7 creative labs, private lesson rooms, practice spaces, a songwriting lounge and a professional recording studio.The building also includes an indoor-outdoor amphitheatre, providing space for performances and gatherings. Students can move between different areas depending on whether they want to practice an instrument, collaborate with other musicians or develop their own compositions.The centre was created to support children and teenagers aged 5 to 18, accommodating beginners as well as those with more advanced musical experience. Its facilities include approximately 250 instruments, among them pianos, trumpets, violins, trombones, drums and other percussion equipment.The building also incorporates vintage musical memorabilia and vinyl records, connecting students with the artists and musical traditions that came before them.A permanent home for the Redding Foundation's music programmesThe centre represents an important development for the Otis Redding Foundation, which had been running music camps and educational programmes without a permanent physical facility of its own.As Georgia Public Broadcasting reported, the foundation had spent years teaching young musicians and songwriters through summer camps and after-school activities. The new building brought those initiatives together in a dedicated environment designed for learning, creativity and performance.The foundation's family members have continued to develop the singer's legacy through education and community programmes. The arts centre gives those efforts a permanent base in the city where Redding's musical journey began.The facility was also made possible through substantial community support. The Macon Melody reported that Zelma Redding, Otis Redding's widow, donated the land for the project, while the foundation raised more than $11 million to construct the building.The opening ceremony took place on March 18, 2025, with community members, local officials and the Redding family gathering at the Zelma Redding Amphitheater to celebrate the completion of the project.What can students learn inside the centreThe facility is intended to provide more than conventional music lessons. Students can explore songwriting, instrument playing, recording, audio mixing and the technical aspects of producing music.According to the Macon Telegraph, experienced musicians and industry professionals are expected to teach students how to play instruments, create sheet music, write lyrics and record audio. The centre also offers opportunities for students to work together, experiment with sounds and develop their own musical ideas.One of its most distinctive features is the O3 Recording Studio, named in memory of Otis Redding III, the singer's son who died in 2023. The studio was designed by engineer Neils Kastor, whose previous work includes recording facilities associated with Katy Perry, P!nk and Dr Dre.The studio incorporates carefully designed acoustic features, including stone walls, a raised concrete floor and specially arranged wooden elements to help produce clear sound. Students can use the professional recording environment to turn their musical ideas into finished recordings.There is a songwriting lounge and soundproof listening spaces, which allow young people to work independently or collaborate without distractions.The centre reaches more than 1,000 students in its first yearThe arts centre's early impact has been reflected in the number of young people who have already benefited from its programmes.In an April 7, 2026 report, the Macon Chamber of Commerce said the centre had served more than 1,000 students through its programmes and school visits during its first year.Karla Redding-Andrews, Otis Redding's daughter, described the progress as particularly meaningful because the facility was created to ensure children could experience the opportunities offered by music and the arts.The centre has also developed into a gathering place for young musicians from across Georgia.A musical legacy rooted in Macon's historyOtis Redding remains one of the most influential figures in soul music. Born in Georgia, the singer became internationally recognised for his powerful voice and songs, including Respect and (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay. He died in a plane crash in December 1967, aged 26.His family's continued investment in music education reflects the importance of giving young people opportunities that he valued during his lifetime.The centre's location also carries personal significance. The facility stands close to places associated with Redding's history in downtown Macon, placing the educational project within the city's wider musical heritage.The building's design deliberately combines contemporary technology with traditional musical experiences. Vinyl records, acoustic instruments and memorabilia sit alongside digital recording equipment and modern creative laboratories, helping students understand both the history and future of music.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran war, inflation or Trump fatigue: What drove Democrats' midterm surge?
articles.summary: US voters on Tuesday delivered a stunning rubuke to President Donald Trump and his broader agenda.
articles.body: US voters on Tuesday delivered a stunning rubuke to President Donald Trump and his broader agenda. From Texas and South Carolina to Ohio and Kansas, Democrats broke through Republican strongholds, overturned seats that had remained out of their reach for decades and made history in several states.The scale of the gains was particularly striking in places Trump had comfortably carried in the 2024 presidential election, suggesting that the voter bloc which helped him return to the White House is beginning to fracture.With Democrats projected to take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, the midterm results represent one of the most significant political reversals of Trump's presidency. But what exactly drove the resurgence? Was it the economic fallout of his policies, the unpopular war with Iran, or growing voter fatigue with the president himself?Inflation, tariffs and Iran war take centre stageThe economy emerged as one of the biggest factors shaping voters' decisions. Trump returned to the White House in 2024 promising to tackle inflation and improve living standards. However, persistent high prices, tariffs on foreign goods and the economic consequences of the war with Iran appear to have undermined that promise.Nearly nine in 10 voters identified the cost of living as a crucial or major factor in their vote, according to exit polls conducted by SSRS for a consortium of US media organisations. Nearly two-thirds blamed Trump for high prices, while around six in 10 said his policies had made the economy worse.The dissatisfaction extended beyond household expenses. Around three-quarters of voters said they were angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country, while concerns about government corruption and Trump's conduct also featured prominently.The war with Iran added another layer of discontent, with voters increasingly questioning the administration's priorities as economic pressures mounted. Trump's attempts to shift attention towards Democratic candidates, portraying them as radical or dangerous, failed to displace the issue that mattered most to many Americans: the cost of everyday essentials.The election also became a referendum on Trump himself. Despite repeatedly urging voters to treat the midterms as a verdict on his presidency, the Republican leader ended up making his party's electoral challenge considerably harder.CNN's voter poll showed that more than six in 10 voters disapproved of Trump's performance, with a majority strongly disapproving. Around six in 10 voters in the AP Voter Poll also believed Trump prioritised his personal interests over those of the country. About 70% wanted Congress to exercise greater checks and balances on the presidency.His intervention in several state-level contests also failed to deliver. Candidates backed by Trump, including Ken Paxton in Texas and Darline Graham in South Carolina, suffered defeats. Republicans also lost ground in states where the president had personally campaigned repeatedly.The Republican coalition that powered Trump's 2024 victory appeared to be weakening. Young voters, Hispanics and other groups that had shifted towards the Republicans two years ago showed signs of moving back towards Democrats. Around seven in 10 voters under 30 supported Democratic candidates in their local House races, while roughly six in 10 Hispanic voters backed Democrats.From Texas to South Carolina: A blue wave beyond expectationsThe Democrats' gains were not confined to traditionally competitive states. Their victories in Republican strongholds underlined the scale of the political shift.In Texas, James Talarico's victory marked the first Democratic Senate win in the state in 38 years. In South Carolina, Annie Andrews defeated Trump's preferred candidate, Darline Graham, delivering Democrats a Senate victory in a state Trump had won by 18 percentage points in 2024.Ohio also delivered a major breakthrough, with Sherrod Brown reclaiming a Republican-held Senate seat and Democrats winning the governor's race. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, ending a Democratic Senate drought stretching back to 1932.The results also produced historic firsts. Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in US history in Georgia, while New Mexico's Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman to win a governorship. New Hampshire's Chris Pappas became the first openly gay male US senator.The Democratic victory, however, comes with limitations. articles.title: Price hikes on the way at Worcester leisure centres
articles.summary: The rises would impact Perdiswell, St John's Sports Centre and Nunnery Wood Sports Complex.
articles.body:
Inflation-busting price increases are on the way at a large Worcester leisure centre, with its operators blaming energy and staffing costs.

The price of an adult swim at Perdiswell Leisure Centre could rise 6.8% – from £7.30 to £7.80 – if the new charges are approved.

Fitness class fees would increase by 5.6% to £9.50, while the price of annual memberships would go up 4.9%.

Bosses at Freedom Leisure, the site's operator, said staffing and energy bills were rising faster than income as Worcester City Council were asked to approve the new prices.

A report on the price hikes, which outstrip the UK's 3.6% inflation rate, revealed energy costs had more than doubled in recent years, despite efforts to slash consumption.

If councillors sign them off in a meeting at the end of November, the average fee at Perdiswell Leisure Centre would increase by 5.3% from January.

Hiring the artificial pitch at Perdiswell, which can currently be done for £44 an hour, would cost 10% more, although the council said it would still be significantly cheaper than comparable pitches elsewhere in the city.

Matt Wickham, Freedom Leisure's chief operating officer, explained the firm had seen "significant cost increases", with gas prices up by more than 50% over the second half of the year and minimum wages rising year-on-year.

"It's really tough because we know people are feeling the pinch in different ways, but our priority is all about offering a value-for-money service to people from all walks of life," he said.

He added the government should consider "immediate financial support" to help the leisure industry through the next 12 months and ongoing investment into leisure centre stock.

If approved, the increases would also apply at St John's Sports Centre and Nunnery Wood Sports Complex, both of which are owned by Freedom Leisure.

Gym-goers at Perdiswell had mixed views on the price increases – with some saying they were not surprised.

Sue Guest said: "I've had two hip replacements so I come and do the aqua swim, it's very beneficial to me.

"It would be a shame if they increase it, but then they (the operators) have their own expenses as well.

"I think it's still reasonable value for money, actually."

Colin English, a pensioner, said: "I use the gym quite a lot, I come at least four or five times a week.

"They put the price up last year – if they do it again by these sorts of amounts I may have to reconsider because it's getting expensive."

Another gym user called Vinny added: "It feels like everything is going up in price at the moment.

"I'd never stop going though, this gym is important to me so I really don't mind."

A final decision is expected to be made on 24 November, subject to discussions at two city council committees before then.
